questions.stem:
Assertion: Cell-mediated immune response is the main protective response against intracellular organisms.
Reason: Cell-mediated immune response causes inactivation of bacteria toxin.
questions.why: T-cells kill infected cells. Cell-mediated responses do not inactivate toxins.

notes.A: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.D: Wrong here: the assertion is true and the reason is false.
notes.E: Wrong here: the assertion is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Adaptive immunity is the first line of defense against viral infections.
Reason: adaptive immunity results in the production of antibodies that block viral infections by preventing viral binding to host cells.
questions.why: Innate immunity is the first line. Antibodies do block binding.

notes.A: Wrong here: the assertion is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the assertion is false.
notes.C: Wrong here: the assertion is false and the reason is true.
notes.E: Wrong here: the reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Antibodies have an important role in containing the spread of a virus in the acute phase of the infection.
Reason: antibodies can eliminate established infections even when the viral genome is integrated into the host chromosomal DNA.
questions.why: Antibodies cannot eliminate integrated viral genomes.

notes.A: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.D: Wrong here: the assertion is true and the reason is false.
notes.E: Wrong here: the assertion is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Sporozoites initiate the major symptoms in malaria.
Reason: sporozoites migrate to the liver where they infect hepatocytes, after which the parasite develops into a multinucleate liver stage (schizont).
questions.why: The merozoite stage causes major symptoms. Sporozoites do target liver cells.

notes.A: Wrong here: the assertion is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the assertion is false.
notes.C: Wrong here: the assertion is false and the reason is true.
notes.E: Wrong here: the reason is true.

questions.stem: Cytokines can be redundant when

options.label: A
options.text: The cytokine has no effect on the cell it acts on

options.label: B
options.text: Cytokine acts on a distant cell

options.label: C
options.text: different cytokines have the same effects

options.label: D
options.text: One cytokine can have different effects on different cells

questions.why: Redundancy means multiple different cytokines can perform the same function.

notes.A: No effect is not redundancy.
notes.B: Acting at a distance is endocrine action.
notes.D: That is pleiotropy.

questions.stem: When a TNF produced by an T helper cell acts on a macrophage to produce IL-1 and TNF, this effect is described as
questions.why: A cytokine stimulating the production of more cytokines creates a cascade.

notes.A: Synergy is two cytokines boosting each other's effect.
notes.C: Redundancy is different cytokines doing the same thing.
notes.D: Pleiotropy is one cytokine with many effects.

questions.stem: Bacteria growing within macrophages are killed by:

options.label: A
options.text: Directly by cytokines released from Th1 cells.

questions.why: Once inside, bacteria are killed by the respiratory burst (ROS) and nitric oxide.

notes.A: Th1 cytokines (IFN-γ) ACTIVATE the macrophage; the macrophage does the killing.
notes.B: Antibodies cannot reach bacteria inside cells.
notes.C: CTLs kill infected cells; macrophage killing uses ROS and NO.

questions.stem: An exotoxin is the only significant virulence factor and is responsible for all the symptoms of the disease in
questions.why: Diphtheria is primarily a toxemia.

notes.B: Shigella dysentery involves invasion of the gut lining, not just a toxin.
notes.C: TB damage comes from intracellular growth and the host response.
notes.D: Strep throat involves invasion and several virulence factors.

questions.stem: Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria avoid innate immunity by

options.label: D
options.text: Living in an immuno-privileged tissue site

questions.why: M. tuberculosis prevents phagosome-lysosome fusion.

notes.B: M. tuberculosis has a waxy mycolic acid wall, not a polysaccharide capsule.
notes.C: Destroying complement is not its main evasion strategy.
notes.D: It lives in macrophages, not in an immune-privileged site.

questions.stem: Extracellular bacteria are optimally killed by:
questions.why: Opsonization by antibodies and complement enhances phagocytosis.

notes.A: Macrophages alone kill less efficiently without opsonins.
notes.B: Complement alone is not optimal.
notes.C: Antibody alone does not kill.

questions.stem: The inappropriate response of immune system towards a relatively harmless antigen causing harm to the host is referred as
questions.why: Hypersensitivity is an exaggerated immune response causing damage.

notes.B: Autoimmunity targets SELF antigens.
notes.C: Immunodeficiency is too LITTLE response.
notes.D: Tolerance is NO response.

questions.stem: Which of the following Ig is involved in mediating allergic reactions
questions.why: IgE binds to mast cells and triggers allergic reactions.

notes.A: IgG mediates type II and III reactions.
notes.B: IgM mediates type II reactions (e.g. ABO).
notes.D: IgA protects mucosa.

questions.stem: ___ is a state of unresponsiveness of the immune system to a potential immunogen
questions.why: Tolerance is the absence of an immune response to a specific antigen.

notes.A: Autoimmunity is a response against self.
notes.B: Immunodeficiency is a failure of the system, not antigen-specific unresponsiveness.
notes.D: Recognition leads to a response.

questions.stem: The major chemical messenger involved in hypersensitivity is
questions.why: Histamine is the primary mediator of immediate hypersensitivity.

notes.A: Interleukins are signalling cytokines, not the main hypersensitivity mediator.
notes.C: Interferons are antiviral.
notes.D: Lysosomes are organelles, not messengers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cell mediated hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.why: Type IV is delayed-type and mediated by T cells.

notes.A: Type I is IgE-mediated.
notes.B: Type II is antibody-mediated (cytotoxic).
notes.C: Type III is immune-complex mediated.

questions.stem: The inability to distinguish self-cells from none-self cells may lead to
questions.why: Autoimmunity occurs when the immune system attacks its own tissues.

notes.A: Hypersensitivity is an excess response to a foreign antigen.
notes.C: Immunodeficiency is too little response.
notes.D: Tolerance is the PROTECTION against attacking self.

questions.stem: Majority of auto immune diseases are
questions.why: Many autoimmune diseases are driven by autoantibodies.

notes.A: Some are T-cell mediated (e.g. type 1 diabetes), but most involve autoantibodies.
notes.C: Macrophages are effectors, not the main driver.
notes.D: Mast cells drive allergy.

questions.stem: All of the following are autoimmune diseases except
questions.why: SCID is an immunodeficiency disorder.

notes.A: Rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune.
notes.C: Graves' disease is caused by TSH-receptor autoantibodies.
notes.D: Addison's disease is autoimmune adrenalitis.

questions.stem: Type I hypersensitivity require which of the following initial priming events to occur?
questions.why: Sensitization is the first exposure where IgE binds to mast cells.

notes.B: The second exposure triggers the reaction; it is not the priming step.
notes.C: Trauma is not required.
notes.D: Degranulation is the effector step, after priming.

questions.stem: Immune modulatory mechanisms employed by pathogens to evade host immune response could include
questions.why: Some pathogens induce tolerance to avoid being attacked.

notes.A: Autoimmunity is a host disorder, not a pathogen strategy.
notes.B: Phagolysosome fusion KILLS pathogens; they try to block it.
notes.D: ROS are host weapons.

questions.stem: Type II hypersensitivity reactions are characterized by
questions.why: Type II is an antibody-mediated cytotoxic reaction.

notes.B: Mast cells drive type I.
notes.C: Red cells may be targets, but they do not characterise the type.
notes.D: Histamine drives type I.

questions.stem: Tumor antigens are ___ that are inappropriately expressed and found on abnormal cells
questions.why: Tumor antigens are often overexpressed self-proteins.

notes.B: Most tumour antigens are altered or overexpressed self-proteins.
notes.C: Antibodies recognise antigens; they are not antigens.
notes.D: T cell receptors recognise antigens.

questions.stem: Cancer results when a mutation leads to which of the following?

options.label: D
options.text: Shut down of the cell cycle

questions.why: Cancer is uncontrolled cell division due to loss of cell-cycle control.

notes.A: Cell death removes cells.
notes.B: Apoptosis protects against cancer.
notes.D: Shutting down the cycle stops growth.

questions.stem: When allergen crosslinks with IgE bound to the Fc receptor on the mast cells... Which of the following receptor have high affinity towards IgE?
questions.why: FcεRI is the high-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells.

notes.B: FcεRII (CD23) is the LOW-affinity receptor.
notes.C: B cell receptors bind antigen, not IgE Fc.
notes.D: TCRs bind peptide–MHC.

questions.stem: A hereditary predisposition of the development of immediate hypersensitivity reaction against common environmental antigens are called
questions.why: Atopy is the genetic tendency to develop allergic diseases.

notes.A: Atrophy is shrinkage of tissue.
notes.C: Anergy is functional unresponsiveness.
notes.D: Synergy is a combined effect.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an example of Type I hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.why: SLE is a Type III hypersensitivity.

notes.A: Asthma is a type I reaction.
notes.B: Allergic rhinitis is a type I reaction.
notes.D: Atopic dermatitis is a type I reaction.

questions.stem: During a blood transfusion, ABO incompatibilities... Which of the following antibody isotype is primarily involved in this type II hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.why: Naturally occurring ABO antibodies are predominantly IgM.

notes.A: IgG causes Rh disease; natural anti-A and anti-B are mainly IgM.
notes.C: IgA does not cause transfusion reactions.
notes.D: IgE drives type I.

questions.stem: Which of the following cytokines are important for DTH and also used of diagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.why: Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) is measured in TB diagnosis.

notes.A: TNF-α helps granulomas but is not measured.
notes.B: TNF-β (lymphotoxin) is not the diagnostic cytokine.
notes.C: IFN-α is mainly antiviral.

questions.stem: Placental tissue is able to evade immune surveillance via
questions.why: Trophoblast cells downregulate classical MHC class I molecules.

notes.B: This helps, but the main mechanism is MHC downregulation.
notes.C: Autoimmunity would harm, not protect.
notes.D: Regulatory T cells are ENHANCED, not exacerbated, and that is not the main evasion route.

questions.stem: A break in tolerance to microbiome could lead to
questions.why: Loss of tolerance to gut microbiota leads to inflammatory bowel diseases.

notes.B: Stomach ulcers are mainly due to H. pylori and NSAIDs.
notes.C: Vomiting is a symptom, not an immune disease.
notes.D: Bronchoconstriction is an airway (type I) response.

questions.stem: Autoimmunity is mostly treated with
questions.why: Corticosteroids are potent immunosuppressants used for autoimmune diseases.

notes.A: Vaccines stimulate immunity.
notes.B: Not a standard treatment for autoimmunity (desensitisation is used for allergy).
notes.C: Antihistamines treat allergy.

questions.stem: True or false: Autoimmunity results when the immune system over reacts.
questions.why: False. Autoimmunity results from a breakdown of tolerance to SELF antigens. An exaggerated response to a harmless foreign antigen is hypersensitivity, not autoimmunity.

questions.stem: True or false: Autoimmunity affects women above 50 years.
questions.why: They frequently affect younger women (e.g., SLE in the 20s and 30s).

questions.stem: True or false: Anergy is a mechanism by which the immune cell induces tolerance.
questions.why: Anergy is a state of functional unresponsiveness.

questions.stem: True or false: Central tolerance occurs in thymus and bone marrow.
questions.why: T cells in the thymus, B cells in the bone marrow.

questions.stem: True or false: Apoptosis is a common mechanism of inducing peripheral tolerance.
questions.why: Activation-induced cell death eliminates autoreactive cells.

questions.stem: True or false: Some drugs and chemical agents can cause autoimmunity.
questions.why: Drugs like procainamide can induce a lupus-like syndrome.

questions.stem: True or false: Histamines are formed by covalent reduction of histidine.
questions.why: Histamine is formed by decarboxylation of histidine.

notes.C: Phosphorylation does not form histamine.
notes.D: Isomerisation does not form histamine.

questions.why: The assertion is true: both affect skin pigmentation. The reason is false as stated: albinism is inherited, but vitiligo is an acquired autoimmune loss of melanocytes (genes only raise susceptibility).

Reason: Tryptophan is a precursor to the neurotransmitter dopamine.
questions.why: Tryptophan is indeed the precursor to serotonin. However, Tyrosine is the precursor to dopamine.

notes.B: Wrong here: the reason is false.

questions.why: Tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin. Its degradation via the kynurenine pathway produces hydroxyanthranilic acid.

notes.B: Histidine gives histamine.

questions.stem:
What is likely to be the complications exhibited by a child with severe combined immunodeficiency:
I. Infection from vaccination
II. Severe cases of yeast infection
III. Comparatively susceptible to infection compared to siblings.
questions.why: Live vaccines are fatal, they get severe fungal/yeast infections, and are highly susceptible to all pathogens.

notes.A: Leaves out II and III, which are also true.
notes.B: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.C: Leaves out I, which is also true.
